title: The Lamps Lit and the Levites Set Apart
summary: Aaron sets up the seven lamps of the golden lampstand so that they shine forward. Then the Levites are cleansed with water, shaving, and washing, presented before the whole congregation, and offered to the LORD as a living wave offering, with the Israelites laying hands on them and sacrifices made for their atonement. The chapter ends with the age limits for Levite service, from twenty-five to fifty, after which older Levites may assist but not carry the heavy work.
story: Chapter 3 announced that God had taken the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn, and chapter 4 assigned their loads. Chapter 8 records the ceremony that actually sets them apart. It is the last major act of preparation before the second Passover in chapter 9 and the departure from Sinai in chapter 10. The chapter begins, perhaps surprisingly, with the lampstand. Its placement is no accident: the light inside the holy place is set to shine forward, and then the people who will serve that holy place are made ready. Everything at Sinai is now nearly in order.
historical:
The lampstand, the menorah, was made according to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain (Exodus 25:31-40), from a single piece of hammered gold with branches shaped like almond blossoms. It stood in the holy place of the tabernacle, and Solomon's temple later had ten lampstands (1 Kings 7:49). After the Romans destroyed the second temple in AD 70, a lampstand from its treasures was carried through Rome in triumph, and the scene is carved on the Arch of Titus, which still stands in the Roman Forum. The menorah became the most widespread symbol of Judaism in antiquity and appears today on the emblem of the State of Israel.

The age limits in verses 24-26 begin at twenty-five, while chapter 4 counted Levites from thirty. Some interpreters see a period of training from twenty-five to thirty; others think the texts reflect practice at different times. By David's reign the starting age had been lowered to twenty (1 Chronicles 23:24-27).
cultural:
The Levites' purification uses the ordinary signs of cleansing in Israel, with special intensity. They are sprinkled with water, shave their entire bodies, and wash their clothes, the same kind of rites required of a person healed of skin disease (Leviticus 14:8-9). Two bulls are offered, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering, and the Levites lay their hands on the animals' heads, the gesture by which a worshiper identified with a sacrifice (Leviticus 1:4).

The most striking act is the reverse of that gesture. The Israelites lay their hands on the Levites (verse 10). The whole people, through representatives, identify with the Levites as a worshiper identifies with an offering, and the Levites are then presented to God as a wave offering. Normally a wave offering was a portion of food, such as the breast of a sacrificed animal, lifted or moved before the altar to show it was given to God and then passed to the priests. Here the offering is a tribe of living men, given to God on behalf of the nation and then passed on to Aaron and his sons as their assistants. The Levites are cleansed, not consecrated with oil like the priests (Leviticus 8:12), which marks the difference between their service and the priests'.
literary: The chapter has three unequal parts, each opened by the formula of God speaking to Moses (verses 1, 5, and 23). The first is brief and puzzlingly placed until we notice that it concerns light shining in front of the lampstand, the inner life of the sanctuary that the Levites will serve. The second follows a pattern common in priestly law, first the command (verses 5-19), then its execution (verses 20-22), with the refrain that everything was done “just as the LORD had commanded Moses.” Inside the command, verses 16-19 restate the reason for the Levites' status from chapter 3 with heavy emphasis: they are wholly given to God, taken in place of the firstborn, and given as a gift to Aaron, and their presence protects Israel from plague. The last part, on age limits, is a practical coda.

doctrines.note: The Levites must be cleansed before they can serve, and the chapter keeps them in a distinct place between the people and the priests. Holiness has degrees, and each is entered by God's appointed means, not by a person's own claim.

Sacrifices make atonement for the Levites (verses 12 and 21), and the Levites in turn serve so that “no plague will come against the Israelites when they approach the sanctuary” (verse 19). The chapter pictures a chain of mediation in which God protects his people through those he appoints to stand between.

The whole congregation takes part in setting the Levites apart by laying hands on them. Those who serve the sanctuary do so on behalf of everyone, and the community owns that service as its own offering to God.

words.note: Menorah, lampstand. It was the only light in the holy place, where there were no windows. Its seven lamps were set to light the area in front of it (verse 2), and the priests kept it burning. The menorah later became the best known symbol of the Jewish people.

Tenuphah, wave offering, from a verb meaning to move back and forth or to lift. Usually it refers to a portion of an offering presented before the altar and then given to the priests. Its use for the Levites themselves (verses 11, 13, 15, 21) is unique and shows that the tribe was, in effect, a living offering from Israel to God.

Samakh, to lean or lay (the hands). Laying hands on an animal identified the worshiper with the sacrifice. Here the Israelites lay hands on the Levites (verse 10), and then the Levites lay hands on the bulls (verse 12). The gesture reappears in the New Testament when the apostles commission the seven in Jerusalem (Acts 6:6).

Taher, to be clean or pure. It describes fitness to approach what is holy, the removal of impurity rather than a gift of new holiness. The Levites are cleansed (verses 6, 7, 15, 21), where the priests were consecrated, and the difference in words marks a difference in office.

christ: Paul urges believers to “offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1), and the Levites are the Old Testament's clearest picture of that idea: living people presented to God as an offering, cleansed, and then put to work. The laying on of hands, used here to set the Levites apart, became the church's gesture for commissioning people to serve (Acts 6:6). The lampstand has its own echo. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and in Revelation John sees “seven golden lampstands” with “One like the Son of Man” standing among them, and learns that the lampstands are the churches (Revelation 1:12-13, 20). Hebrews also cites the instruction about the lampstand's pattern, “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Hebrews 8:5), to argue that the tabernacle was a copy of heavenly realities fulfilled in Christ. These are connections the New Testament draws by taking up the tabernacle's patterns, not predictions made by this chapter.
questions: The Levites were given to God on behalf of the whole people, and the people laid hands on them. How does your community share in the work of those it sets apart for service?
The lamps were set to shine forward, lighting the space before them. What does it mean for a life of worship to give light to what is around it?
Levites over fifty stopped carrying heavy loads but kept helping their brothers. What might that pattern teach about changing roles in service as we age?
